FAST

NEW YORK, Oct 29 : The US filed a lawsuit on Thursday accusing Google of failing to give an employee his old job back or put him in a similar job after he returned from a year of military leave as a US Army reservist. According to a complaint filed in Manhattan federal court, Mark Davisson spent 2-1/2 years as a Google key account executive, where he handled accounts for the asset manager BlackRock, hedge fund Bridgewater Associates and the former Credit Suisse. Upon Davisson's return from leave in May 2023, the Alphabet unit allegedly refused to let Davisson handle any customer accounts, though he kept his pay and title, depriving him of possible career advancement. The complaint said Google later assigned Davisson to a cloud solutions position that also involved no managing of customer accounts, and fired him in August 2024 as part of a broader workforce reduction. Google did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK/LONDON, Oct 29 : The euro edged higher on Thursday after the European Central Bank kept interest rates unchanged, while the dollar eased against most major currencies in the wake of data showing rising US inflation. The ECB left interest rates unchanged in a well-telegraphed move but warned that inflation risks were on the rise from surging energy costs. The central bank also announced the early departure of President Christine Lagarde, who will step down on February 7, ahead of the end of her tenure in October 2027. The euro fell to its lowest against the dollar since May but was last up 0.11 per cent on the day at around $1.1163. The euro weakened 0.23 per cent against the pound to 0.834.  "As expected, the ECB leaves rates unchanged at today’s meeting, but signals that a rate hike in December is firmly in play, citing upside risks to the inflation outlook," said Marchel Alexandrovich, European economist at Saltmarsh Economics.

"The bigger news is the confirmation that Christine Lagarde will leave her post in February, rather than in October of next year. Markets will not be surprised by the announcement, but it will bring into focus the fact that the ECB is heading for a significant reshuffle in the first half of 2027, with Isabel Schnabel, Lagarde, and Philip Lane — the ECB’s de facto chief economist — all set to depart imminently." US Commerce Department data showed that inflation accelerated in September as consumers paid more for gasoline and other goods, supporting economists' expectations of an interest rate increase from the Federal Reserve in December. The US economy, however, grew faster than expected in the third quarter, helped by resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment, data also showed. The Fed had opted to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week's midterm elections. The dollar has not reacted significantly to the latest economic events largely because much of it had been as expected and had already been priced in, said Eugene Epstein, head of structured products for Moneycorp North America. The dollar weakened 0.13 per cent to 0.827 against the Swiss franc. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh had said that inflation can be lowered to the 2 per cent target without having to "throw sand in the gears" and slow growth or raise unemployment, pushing traders to rein in bets for rate hikes in 2027. Warsh also said the central bank would begin setting aside one of its eight regular policy meetings next year and two in 2028 to discuss major issues facing the institution and would not use them to consider changes in monetary policy. Still, markets are pricing in a nearly 80 per cent chance of a rate hike in December, according to the CME's FedWatch tool. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.08 per cent to 102.02. BOJ DECISION IN FOCUS Attention is also on the Bank of Japan, which concludes a two-day meeting on Friday and is expected to keep rates steady. The Japanese yen weakened 0.04 per cent against the greenback to 157.87 per dollar.   The New Zealand dollar was flat at $0.5625, having slumped nearly 2 per cent following the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's surprise decision on Wednesday to keep rates at 2.75 per cent.

Source: Reuters

FAST

LONDON, Oct 29 : Major central banks took a break from interest rates rises this week, but they are by no means done, with energy prices near multi-month highs and no resolution to the conflict in the Middle East in sight. The Federal Reserve and European Central Bank both kept rates steady this week, but signaled with inflation above target they still have work to do. The ECB is also in focus as President Christine Lagarde announced she would step down early. The Bank of Japan is likely to stay on hold later this week, but next week's central bank meetings should see hikes, including from the Bank of England, its first of 2026. Here's where central banks in the Group of 10 developed economies stand, ranked from highest to lowest policy rate.

1/ AUSTRALIA The Reserve Bank of Australia has hiked interest rates four times this year. Their next policy decision is on November 3, and markets see a high chance of another hike, boosted by a hot inflation print and hawkish comments from governor Michele Bullock. 2/ NORWAY Norges Bank also meets next week after catching markets off guard with a hike in May and repeating the move in September, when it left the door open for additional tightening. Its annual core inflation held at 3.0 per cent in September, slightly above the central bank's 2.9 per cent forecast. 3/ UNITED STATES The Federal Reserve left rates unchanged on Wednesday ahead of next week's U.S. midterm elections while awaiting further evidence on inflation, which “remained elevated.” President Donald Trump has repeatedly called for rate cuts and recently accused policymakers of being "hostile" and "partisan" after September's rate increase. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh rejected those accusations, stressing the central bank's independence. Traders price 80 per cent chance of a hike in December and see at least one, likely two, further moves in 2027. 4/ BRITAIN The Bank of England has not raised rates this year so far, but that will likely change next week. Markets are almost fully pricing a hike, backed by recent data including hotter-than-expected September inflation and a pickup in wage growth. Governor Andrew Bailey has long warned the likelihood of a hike grows the longer energy prices stay high. 5/ NEW ZEALAND The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised on Wednesday by keeping its benchmark official cash rate at 2.75 per cent in a narrow vote rather than hiking for the third time in a row. Governor Anna Breman said on Thursday chances the bank will hike the official cash rate in December are "high" Markets see roughly an 80 per cent probability of that. 6/ EURO AREA The European Central Bank delivered what market participants deem a hawkish hold, leaving rates unchanged but warning that inflation risks were rising. The central bank's most immediate challenge is the sharp rise in France's debt risk premium, driven by growing investor concerns over the country's debt burden and uncertain fiscal trajectory President Christine Lagarde resigned on Thursday so she could weigh in on political matters in France and globally. 7/ CANADA The Bank of Canada raised its key rate for the first time in more than three years on Wednesday, as widely expected, but Governor Tiff Macklem said policy remained slightly accommodative. The central bank hiked by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, still below the 2.75 per cent the BoC estimates is neither restrictive nor expansionary for the economy. The BoC also raised its inflation forecast for 2027 to 3.1 per cent from the 2.0 per cent predicted in July. 8/ SWEDEN Sweden's Riksbank, long in the dovish camp, now looks set for a rate hike, with markets pricing around an 80 per cent chance of one next week. Sweden's central bank chief earlier this month said that there was a strong case for a hike as the economy has been performing better than expected, and the risk of inflation overshooting its target has grown. 9/ JAPAN The Bank of Japan is set to keep rates steady this week. But, the central bank is expected to signal its readiness to keep raising borrowing costs, and sources told Reuters that it may also raise its inflation forecast. Recent data has pointed to broadening price pressures. Markets however aren't fully pricing in another hike from the BOJ until January 2027. 10/ SWITZERLAND The Swiss National Bank (SNB) is set to keep its policy rate at 0 per cent for the coming months. Minutes of its September meeting showed policymakers thought monetary conditions are "appropriate" to keep inflation within its target range over the medium term. Low yields should prevent the franc currency from appreciating too sharply, even though geopolitical tensions have often driven investors towards safe-haven assets in 2026.

Source: Reuters

Oct 29 : French AI startup Mistral released its Large 4 model to the public on Thursday, saying it was designed to help organisations identify and fix cyber-security vulnerabilities. Unlike leading AI systems such as Google's Gemini, which are mainly accessed through online services, the model can be downloaded and run independently by anyone. Mistral said the released version was an upgrade from the one unveiled three weeks ago, following testing with governments and corporate users, which helped improve its performance. The company said organisations could use the software on their own systems, reducing dependence on a third-party provider.

FAST

Oct 29 : Alphabet is making billions of dollars selling homegrown AI chips it once reserved for internal use, but building inventory to meet surging demand is draining cash as the tech giant spends heavily on data centres. Unlike its traditional search and cloud businesses, selling AI chips that compete with Nvidia's requires Alphabet to spend on hardware well before customers pay, putting pressure on cash flow. The trade-off, outlined by finance chief Anat Ashkenazi on Alphabet's post-earnings call on Wednesday, offers an early look at the costs of a business that has emerged as one of the company's biggest growth areas as investors fret over AI's threat to its lucrative search advertising business. "Where previously inventory balances were primarily some of our hardware products, now those TPU (custom chip) systems that are not yet sold will be showing up. So you see cash going out ... it's not the traditional kind of capex but rather a different cycle of cash flow generation," Ashkenazi said.

That shift could pressure Alphabet just as investors grow more concerned about the mounting cost of AI. Its shares fell nearly 11 per cent on Thursday after the company reported another quarter of cash burn and reiterated that spending on AI infrastructure would rise sharply next year. Still, the processors are helping drive growth. Alphabet does not break out revenue or margins from the chips, called tensor processing units, but said their sales made a "meaningful" contribution as Google Cloud revenue more than doubled in the September quarter. Sales of TPU systems, which bundle the chips with networking, storage and software, are expected to rise further in the current quarter and ramp up significantly in 2027, Google Cloud chief Thomas Kurian said. Alphabet last year said it would supply Anthropic with TPUs worth tens of billions of dollars. Media reports have said the company is also in talks on a similar deal with OpenAI. "We completely think these are short-term gyrations," said Jeremy Saltzberg, senior investment officer at Check Capital. "We don't have reason to believe that the margins would be significantly different than what an Nvidia GPU (graphic processing unit) would sell for. And of course, Nvidia GPU margin is incredible."

FAST

HELSINKI, Oct 29 : Finnish police said on Thursday they had launched a criminal investigation into suspected breaches of environmental law at the construction site of a planned Google data centre in northern Finland. The project is part of a plan announced last month by Alphabet's Google to invest $15 billion in artificial intelligence infrastructure in Finland, which the US company described as its largest investment in Europe. Authorities have said Tuike Finland, a subsidiary of Alphabet's Google, conducted forest clearing and drainage at a planned site near the town of Muhos before the environmental impact assessments required under Finnish law had been completed. A Google spokesperson said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites.

POLICE PROBE DRAINAGE AND WATER MANAGEMENT "We are investigating whether the company's operations have breached the water act and resulted in environmental damage," Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen told Reuters, adding that a guilty finding could lead to a corporate fine. Pakanen declined to say whether any individuals could become a target of the investigation. Preliminary information showed ambiguities and shortcomings in the drainage and water management at Tuike's site, police said in a statement, adding that they would give an update in December but that the investigation would extend into 2027. On October 6, Finland's Supervisory Agency (LVV), which oversees environmental permits and assessments, ordered Google to halt preparatory measures altering the environment at Muhos as well as a separate site. It is up to regulator LVV to decide on any permits to restart the work at the data centre sites, Pakanen said. An LVV spokesperson said it was unclear how long it might take before the agency grants the relevant permits. "We've partnered closely with the government and communities in Finland on infrastructure for over a decade, and are actively responding to enquiries from LVV and other authorities," the Google spokesperson said. FINLAND'S APPEAL FOR DATA CENTRE INVESTMENT Finland's cool climate, low-carbon electricity and government endorsement of AI projects have contributed to making the country one of Europe's main destinations for data centre investments in recent years. Finland, similar in size to Germany but with a population of less than 6 million people, has had less vocal opposition to data centre buildouts than other places, including in the United States. AI data centres are among the main drivers of a projected rise of up to 40 per cent in Finland's electricity consumption in the coming years, if all agreed grid connection projects go ahead, grid operator Fingrid has said. Google's planned investments in Finland include data centres, electricity grid improvements and clean energy and battery projects to power services such as Gemini, Search, Maps and YouTube. Supporting Google's plan, Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo last month said that the deal would be a boost for the economy, playing down concerns it would suck up energy and push up power prices. The prime minister's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Source: Reuters

Oct 29 : Serval raised $150 million in a Sequoia-led round at a $3 billion valuation, as the enterprise automation company seeks to use AI agents to handle workplace tasks and replace legacy software across large organizations. The round triples Serval's $1 billion valuation from December, highlighting investor interest in AI startups taking on established enterprise software providers such as ServiceNow and Workday. San Francisco-based Serval, which has raised $277 million to date, develops AI agents that automate workplace processes, initially focusing on IT operations such as managing employee access, troubleshooting, and handling software and hardware assets. "It's not an additional layer of AI spend on top of your existing system of record, it is a true alternative replacement for platforms like ServiceNow," Jake Stauch, co-founder and CEO of Serval, told Reuters.

On how companies can prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive information or making unauthorized changes, Stauch said Serval separates the agent used by administrators to build tools from the one employees use to access approved workflows. He said permissions and approvals are controlled by IT and security teams, while customers still generally want human approval for sensitive actions such as password resets, application access and changes to sensitive systems. Previous investors, including Elad Gil, First Round and General Catalyst, also joined the latest funding round.

LONDON, Oct 29 : Britain's financial regulator has secured a court-backed agreement with cryptocurrency exchange HTX that will bar it from knowingly promoting cryptoasset services unlawfully to UK customers, the watchdog said on Thursday. The Financial Conduct Authority had in October 2025 sued HTX — formerly known as Huobi and one of the world's largest crypto platforms – over alleged illegal UK promotions. Regulators and authorities around the world have for years warned that nascent crypto markets – which are generally less regulated than mainstream financial markets – present risks to investors. The FCA's first High Court battle against an overseas crypto firm over marketing to UK consumers highlights how some authorities are trying to police global crypto companies that can have opaque corporate structures and ignore them – while reaching customers via the Internet.

FRANKFURT, Oct 29 : European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation on Thursday, ending months of speculation about her future at a complex juncture for Europe and the ECB. Lagarde will step down on February 7, giving current European Union leaders time to pick a successor well before a French presidential election that polls show far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favourite to win. "European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today informed the Governing Council and the President of the European Council António Costa that she will step down from her position on 7 February 2027," the ECB said in a press release. The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are seen as frontrunners to replace Lagarde.

The move comes as the ECB is in the middle of a rate-hiking cycle, seeking to prevent an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages. But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields — especially in debt-laden France — that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation. Caught between persistent inflation fuelled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5 per cent on Thursday while signalling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely. WASHINGTON, Oct 29 : Voters in 10 US states will decide on Election Day whether to curb data center development in their communities, as the rapid buildout needed to power the AI boom stirs local opposition. Resistance is especially visible in Ohio, one of the country's fastest-growing data center markets. No state has more data center-related ballot measures, with voters in more than a dozen jurisdictions set to consider 21 proposals alongside Tuesday's midterm elections, according to the nonpartisan research group Ballotpedia.  Voters in 38 local jurisdictions will consider at least 41 measures that would delay, prohibit or impose new requirements on data centers, the sprawling facilities that provide the computing power required to run AI applications.  Most states require petition drives or other demonstrations of public support before measures can qualify for the ballot, and their appearance reflects growing data center opposition across the political spectrum. Support for banning construction of certain data centers is coming from both Democrats and Republicans, said local organizer Jessica Baker. "We all want the same thing."

Baker, who is part of the advocacy group Conserve Ohio, said concerns about data centers' electricity and water demands are driving the opposition. Even if developers generate their own power through gas turbines or nuclear reactors, many residents still do not want the facilities built near their communities because they are worried about health risks to their kids, such as asthma, she said. If Ohio voters approve restrictions, developers are likely to steer projects elsewhere rather than abandon them altogether, said Baron Fung, who oversees IT infrastructure research at market research firm Dell'Oro Group. The industry already contends with major obstacles, including years-long waits for grid connections and rising construction costs. “If there’s a cancellation or delay in certain sites, (developers) can potentially shift some of that demand to another site,” Fung said. FULL STEAM AHEAD Recent growth suggests local opposition has not meaningfully slowed the industry. US data center capacity under construction increased 48 per cent from December 2025 to June 2026, measured in gigawatts, according to John McWilliams, head of data center insights at real estate services firm Cushman & Wakefield.  “Even though there are areas or jurisdictions around the country where there is some friction between developers, there’s still areas where projects are moving forward,” McWilliams said. The ballot measures have drawn attention from some of the industry's largest players. In Sunbury, near Columbus, a measure that would ban data centers that use more than 25 megawatts of power could derail Amazon's proposed $2 billion data center development. Amazon's public policy lead Shannon Kellogg appeared on local television in October to answer questions about the project ahead of the vote.  An Amazon spokesperson declined to say whether the ballot initiatives across the US would affect the company's data center expansion plans.  "We're focused on working with local residents and officials to build data centers that support jobs, strengthen local economies through millions in tax payments and power the technologies customers rely on," the spokesperson said. "Regardless of the outcome of any single measure, our commitment to the communities where we operate remains the same."

TOKYO, Oct 29 : Japan can tap more of the huge surplus in its foreign exchange special account to fund spending, private-sector members of a key government panel said on Thursday, arguing it already has sufficient buffers to withstand sharp moves in the yen. The proposal, made at a meeting of the Council on Economic and Fiscal Policy, comes as policymakers debate ways to secure funding for tax cuts and spending plans without adding to the country's already huge debt pile. Japan should "accurately assess and secure" non-tax revenues and money left unused from state funds, the members said in a proposal that lays the groundwork for the government's budget drafting for the next fiscal year starting on April 1. The surplus in Japan's foreign exchange special account, in particular, should be "actively used" as a source of funding for spending, the proposal said.

Japan holds roughly $1.2 trillion in foreign reserves, which include US Treasuries, in a special account that is used to conduct currency intervention. The surplus in the account has increased due to the yen's depreciation, which inflates the yen-denominated value of US Treasuries, and interest payments from the foreign assets. The finance ministry sets guidelines on the ratio of surplus funds that should be retained in the account, to ensure it has enough foreign assets to sell when it needs to conduct interventions aimed at propping up the yen against other currencies. "Assuming currency rates remain around current levels, Japan has sufficient buffers against exchange-rate risks for the time being," the members said, adding that Japan can tap more money from the special account without breaching the guidelines. Japan spent 15 trillion yen ($95 billion) on interventions between July 30 and August 26 to prop up the yen, leading to the biggest-ever drop in its foreign reserves in August. The possibility of tapping the account has drawn attention as a potential means of funding Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's planned two-year cut in the consumption tax rate for food items, which is estimated to cost roughly 5 trillion yen per year. The administration's big spending plans triggered a spike in bond yields in July by stoking fears of increased debt issuance that would worsen Japan's already tattered finances. Since then, Takaichi has stressed the administration's resolve to pursue "responsible" fiscal policy and curb debt issuance by tapping non-tax revenues and reviewing existing subsidies and proceeds from special accounts and state funds. The administration has also vowed to discontinue the practice of compiling an extra budget each year, beyond the annual budget, to fund big stimulus packages. But in a sign the pledge could be watered down, the private-sector panel members said Japan should not rule out compiling an extra budget when fiscal spending is needed to deal with economic shocks. ($1 = 157.8700 yen)

PARIS, Oct 29 : Meta Platforms has lost its appeals against interim measures imposed by French regulators over media organisations' publishing rights in the Paris Court of Appeals, the court said on Thursday. Tech companies and publishers have been involved in a growing number of cases under litigation over content published on social media or used for AI training. Under European Union law, print media are allowed to seek payment for the digital use of their content and France has sought to strictly enforce the EU rules. A previous agreement between Meta and press associations determining the amount due expired in 2024, and the two sides have since failed to agree. French media have received no payment since 2025.

Oct 29 : Nasdaq futures dropped on Thursday as mixed earnings from Alphabet and Microsoft left investors weighing the payoff from heavy AI spending, with focus also on an inflation reading a day after the Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged. Alphabet slid 10.5 per cent in premarket trading after the company reported disappointing results in the core business of search advertising and a massive acceleration in cash burn as it poured resources into building out AI. "Investors are starting to scrutinize monetization timelines versus the capital expenditure burn rates. Some investors are no longer giving all hyperscalers a 'free pass' to spend without limit," said Jeremy Saltzberg, VP and senior investment officer at Check Capital Management. On the other hand, Microsoft climbed 3.5 per cent after the company delivered a big cash-flow beat and forecast strong cloud growth, offering fresh evidence that its hefty AI bets were working.

Other early movers included cybersecurity firm Fortinet, which tumbled 25.4 per cent after reporting third-quarter results. Software maker ServiceNow dropped 19 per cent after missing third-quarter profit estimates. Other software-related companies, including Zscaler and Salesforce, were among the laggards in sector-wide weakness. Marvell Technology fell 9.4 per cent after media reports said the company is in advanced talks to buy data-center optics maker Lumentum Holdings. Lumentum shares rose 4.3 per cent. Marvell and Lumentum did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. The broader semiconductor space was trading lower, with Nvidia down 1 per cent, AMD sliding 3.3 per cent and Intel off 3.6 per cent. Intel and Amazon are some of the major tech companies reporting after markets close on Thursday. On the earnings docket before the bell are drugmakers Merck and Eli Lilly, construction equipment maker Caterpillar, and alternative investment managers Ares Management and Blue Owl. At 4:09 a.m. ET, Dow E-minis were up 185 points, or 0.35 per cent, and S&P 500 E-minis were down 31 points, or 0.41 per cent. Nasdaq 100 E-minis were down 365 points, or 1.22 per cent. Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week's US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation. "The decision to hold seems to be a short pause to assess ahead of a likely policy hike in December, rather than an indication that no further tightening is needed," said Jon Butcher, a senior US economist at Aberdeen. Focus will be on the September Personal Consumption Expenditures report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, due later in the day. A third-quarter GDP reading is also set for release. Traders currently see a more than 81 per cent chance the Fed will hike interest rates in December, as per the CME FedWatch Tool, as key inflation metrics remain elevated amid the oil shock caused by the Middle East conflict. Money market participants are also pricing an additional rate hike by mid-2027, according to data compiled by LSEG. Among other stocks, car e-commerce platform Carvana jumped 9.2 per cent after its third-quarter revenue surpassed estimates, while Chipotle Mexican Grill gained 6.7 per cent after reporting better-than-expected quarterly comparable sales.

Source: Reuters

Oct 29 : STMicroelectronics raised its 2026 forecast for AI data centre revenue on Thursday, after demand from data centres and satellite operators helped it beat market expectations for third-quarter earnings. The Franco-Italian chipmaker now expects to book about $1.3 billion in data centre revenue in 2026, up from a July forecast of more than $1 billion. It reiterated the 2027 goal of well above $2 billion. CEO Jean-Marc Chery told analysts demand was driven mainly by STMicro's silicon photonics chips, which use light rather than electrical signals to move data between servers. The company's quarterly operating income excluding one-off charges was $429 million, nearly doubling from a year ago and beating the $400.5 million expected by analysts polled by LSEG.

It forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $4.15 billion, up from $3.76 billion in the third quarter, give or take 3.5 per cent. Analysts had expected $4.10 billion. "In an environment where demand remains well above supply, we continue to expand capacity," Chery said in the earnings statement. STMicro, which makes chips ranging from microcontrollers to sensors and power semiconductors for cars, factories and smartphones, said higher sales of communication equipment, computer peripherals and personal electronics drove the beat. It had said already in July that fourth-quarter sales would be more than $4 billion. Chery said on Thursday that company-specific drivers, including data centre demand and low-Earth-orbit satellite communications, were adding to the cyclical recovery. The company's gross margin rose to 37.3 per cent in the third quarter from 33.2 per cent a year ago, helped by a higher share of sales from more profitable chips and lower costs from idle factory capacity. STMicro expects the margin to rise to about 39 per cent in the fourth quarter. STMicro shares opened 3.7 per cent lower but quickly recovered to trade slightly positive by 0935 GMT.

Source: Reuters

HANOI, Oct 29 : Vietnam's top miner Vinacomin plans to keep coal output at 40 million metric tons per year through 2030 to meet domestic demand, mostly for power generation, state media reported on Thursday. • The company will develop 18 mining projects in the northern province of Quang Ninh province to maintain the output, reported Vietnam News Agency • Vinacomin will also import 10 million to 20 million tons of coal a year to meet demand • Coal remains a key fuel source for Vietnam's thermal power plants and broader energy security goals • "Ensuring an adequate coal supply for thermal power plants plays a core role in maintaining the operation of the power system and safeguarding national energy security," the company was quoted as saying • Vinacomin is among the companies in which the state will maintain 100 per cent ownership until at least 2030

Source: Reuters

TOKYO, Oct 29 : Japanese government bonds (JGBs) were steady on Thursday, a day before the Bank of Japan's monetary policy decision, while strong demand at an auction of 2-year notes provided support. The market was also buoyed by gains in US Treasuries after the Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged and gave few signals about the chances of a hike at the next meeting in December. "The market seemed to perceive it as less hawkish than expected," said Yuhi Kawano, a market analyst at Mizuho Securities. "Under these circumstances, it’s easy to see why the need for the Bank of Japan to raise rates at a high pace seems low, which should be supportive for the yen bond market."
